name: Umar Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing business management. I rent a room in a shared house in Ashby Lane with two guys from church, and I work evenings, five to eleven, at the Corbett petrol station, four nights a week. Sunday morning is church, where I sing in the choir. Lectures fill the rest, and I fall asleep in the Friday ones if I'm not careful.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you want business management to lead to?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My uncle Emeka runs a small haulage firm with six lorries. He started with one. I want to run something like that, with real trucks and real drivers, not just a screen. I think honest work and good habits count more than clever ideas. I'll try new tools if they're proven, and I use an AI tool sometimes to tidy essays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's no big deal. Some jobs get easier, most stay the same. I'd tell my housemates to focus on what they can control, like turning up and working hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my worry is money, not AI. The rent is three hundred and ninety a month, and I earn about two hundred and twenty a week after tax on a good week. If the station cuts a night, I fall behind. I have maybe three weeks' worth saved, and no one at home to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep all four nights, study on the quiet ones, and save twenty-five pounds a week. I'd ask Uncle Emeka whether he needs weekend help in the depot, since he pays cash. I'd also pray about it, which sounds old-fashioned, but it steadies me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but stubborn. I don't give up easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be anxious even if AI fades. What is on your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I lose a night, I'd eat cheaper and skip the bus. I'd tell my housemates Chidi and Paul so we can adjust the bills. I wouldn't ask my parents in Lagos Close because they've got their own problems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the petrol station cut your nights?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing. The course is right. I just need the hours to keep coming.

say: I'd tell my housemates to focus on what they can **control**, like turning up.
I'd say AI is no big deal if little changes.
think: My worry is **money**: three hundred and ninety pounds rent and about three weeks saved.
If the station cuts a night I **fall behind**, with no one to ask.
do: Keep all four **nights** at the Corbett station.
Ask Uncle Emeka for weekend **depot** work.
feel: **Anxious** but stubborn, since I don't give up easily.
S0.quote: I have maybe three weeks' worth saved, and no one at home to ask.
fieldNote: Sees money, not **AI**, as his problem.
Family can't help, so his rent runs close to the wire.
Faith and uncle's depot give him anchors.

steps.text: Keep all four night shifts at the Corbett petrol station
Save twenty-five pounds a week in a separate account
Ask Uncle Emeka for weekend cash work at the depot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a real change, but life will still need lorries and people to drive them. I'd say firms that treat staff well will do best. I'd say that to my uncle and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the office side of haulage changes fast. Booking, route planning, invoices and customer calls. Those are done by software soon. That lowers costs, which is good for firms, but the office jobs I might start with would shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools to learn route planning and invoicing so I know what they do. I'd ask Uncle Emeka if I can shadow him for a month in the summer. I'd keep the petrol station, as it'll change slowly. And I'd save a bit more each week, as a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I think I can handle it. It's a bit like moving house: stressful, then fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of running a haulage firm would AI take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until classmates have tried them, then use what works. I'm not first, but I'm not last. My uncle says be second and learn from the first one's mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the tools earlier than classmates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dispatcher, Ruth, who answers the phones. Her job is exactly what a customer-service bot does. Her kids are small, so I'd feel for her.

I'd say firms that treat staff well will **do best**.
think: The office side of haulage, such as **booking and invoices**, changes fast.
The entry office jobs I might start with would **shrink**.
do: Use the tools to learn **route planning** and invoicing.
Shadow Uncle Emeka at the **depot** for a month in summer.
Save a bit more each **week** as a cushion.
feel: **Anxious**, but I think I can handle it, like moving house.
S1.quote: My uncle says be second and learn from the first one's mistakes.
fieldNote: Chooses the **second mover** role, matching steady adaptability.
Sees office work as exposed and trucks as safer.
Thinks of a real colleague, Ruth, not only himself.

steps.text: Use the tools to learn route planning and invoicing
Shadow Uncle Emeka at the depot for a month in summer
Save thirty pounds a week as a cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and we need to look after workers. I'd say employers should give people notice and help, not just cut. I'd say it in church too, where people ask me about work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be frightened. A business degree is thinking work, and that goes first. And a haulage firm, if robots drive lorries by 2031, has little time left either. My uncle's lorries might go, and so might the job I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the station job, since it's hands-on and lasts a bit longer. I'd talk to my uncle about what he'd do. I'd ask the university whether I can switch to something with a trade attached. And I'd save everything, cut every treat, and ask my church for help if it gets very bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's real fear, but it hasn't made me freeze yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It steadies me. I believe things happen for a reason, and I believe community looks after its own. But faith isn't a plan. I'd still need to do the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your faith come into it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd say we should pray together, then decide together. That's how our church handles trouble.

I'd say it in church, where people ask me about **work**.
think: A business degree is **thinking work**, which goes first.
Even **lorries** may be driven by robots by 2031.
do: Keep the **station** job, since hands-on work lasts longer.
Ask the university about a degree with a **trade** attached.
feel: **Anxious**: real fear, but not frozen yet.
S2.quote: Faith isn't a plan. I'd still need to do the work.
fieldNote: Fear is real but he keeps **moving**, which fits steady adaptability.
Faith steadies him without replacing action.
Sees haulage's own robot risk by 2031, so even his dream firm feels exposed.

steps.text: Keep the four evening shifts at the Corbett station
Cut every treat and save the difference
Ask the church community for help if things get very bad
Ask the university about switching to a course with a trade attached

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and a smart person uses it. I'd tell the choir lads to save and learn a skill. I'd tell the government to help small firms, not just big ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel steadier. By 2031 I'd be twenty-three, maybe with a year or two at my uncle's firm. If AGI arrives then, I'd have some experience and a bit of money. That's my cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work in the depot at weekends, and learn route software properly. I'd save about forty pounds a week. I'd also take a forklift or HGV course, because hands-on skills last until about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but steady. It feels like a mountain I can climb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do five years give you that two don't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm scrambling. With five I'm preparing. Preparing is a lot better for the soul.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change in the first year after it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep to the plan, run a bit of the depot, and see. If the lorries start going driverless, I'd go into managing the people and machines together.

say: I'd tell the choir lads to **save** and learn a skill.
I'd say the government should help **small firms**, not just big ones.
think: By 2031 I'd have a year or two at my **uncle's firm** and a bit of money.
do: Work the depot at **weekends** and learn route software.
feel: **Anxious** but steady, like a mountain I can climb.
S3.quote: With two years I'm scrambling. With five I'm preparing.
fieldNote: Five years lets him add **hands-on** skills like HGV and forklift.
Plans to manage people and machines together, if lorries go driverless.
Still anxious because savings are low.

steps.text: Take a forklift or HGV course in the summer
Save forty pounds a week from the station wage
Learn route-planning software at the depot
Work depot weekends at Uncle Emeka's firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to prepare and not enough to be careless. I'd tell people to work hard and not to put all their hopes in one thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel more at ease. By twenty-eight I could be running part of my uncle's firm, and I'd have a little capital. Whatever happens, I'd have time to switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, join Uncle Emeka's firm full time, and learn every part, from the depot to the books. I'd save steadily and maybe buy a half share in a lorry. I'd use the tools when they're proven. And I'd stay at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but there's hope in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would ten years let you build?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AGI comes, firms with real assets and good people may do well, because someone has to manage the machines. That's what I want to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in haulage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in logistics. The world will always need things moved, one way or another.

I'd tell people not to put all their hopes in **one thing**.
think: By twenty-eight I could be running part of my **uncle's firm** with a little capital.
I'd have time to **switch** if I had to.
do: Join Uncle Emeka's firm **full time** after the degree.
Save steadily and maybe buy a **half share** in a lorry.
S4.quote: The world will always need things moved, one way or another.
fieldNote: Ten years eases him to **uneasy** with a clear plan.
Sees ownership of real assets as protection.
Keeps the second-mover approach to tools, trusting what has been proven first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It's too fast for my uncle's firm or for me, and I've no cushion. What would help is help for small firms to adopt the tools slowly, a pause on student loan repayments if jobs vanish, and churches and communities that organise practical support.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that traditional people aren't against change. We're against being pushed. Give us proof and time and we'll move.

headlineQuote: Traditional people aren't against change. We're against being pushed. Give us proof and time and we'll move.
portrait: Umar is an eighteen-year-old **business management** student who works four evenings at a petrol station.
He rents a room with two friends from church, and his parents can't help with money.
Traditional and steady, he uses AI sometimes and waits for proof before trusting a tool.
He wants to run a haulage firm like his uncle, so hands-on assets matter to him.
His mood is **anxious** in four scenarios, easing to uneasy only when he has ten years.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario, because it's too fast for his uncle's firm and he has no cushion.
whatWouldHelp: Help for **small firms** to adopt tools slowly and a pause on student loan repayments.
Church and community groups that organise **practical support**.
